scenes.tts: These two G F P filled vesicles are one hundred fifty nanometres apart. An ordinary light microscope records one spot. Why can software zoom not split it back into two? Follow the light from specimen to screen, and watch where the missing detail is lost.
scenes.caption: These two GFP-filled vesicles are 150 nanometres apart. An ordinary light microscope records one spot. Why can software zoom not split it back into two? Follow the light from specimen to screen, and watch where the missing detail is lost.
scenes.visual: Open directly on one continuous optical bench filling the frame: two green cartoon vesicles inside a dark cell at left, a large blue objective in the centre, and a detector screen at right. A yellow bracket between vesicle centres reads '150 nm'. Green emission ripples continuously from both vesicles toward the lens. The screen begins with two tiny source markers, then transforms into one broad red-labelled spot as the question lands. Mark the entire picture 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: These two GFP-filled vesicles are 150 nanometres apart. An ordinary light microscope records one spot. Why can software zoom not split it back into two? Follow the light from specimen to screen, and watch where the missing detail is lost.

scenes.visual: Keep the same bench and ambient green emission ripples. Dim it slightly and place the title 'What Zoom Cannot Recover' across the upper third for two seconds, then clear the title without moving the bench.

scenes.tts: Start with one point source. In ideal widefield fluorescence, every point becomes a blur. The screen shows a bright centre with faint rings, an Airy pattern. This computed green curve is its intensity across the screen.
scenes.visual: Temporarily dim the upper vesicle while leaving it visible. Let light from the lower green point travel through the blue objective. On the same detector, build a computed Airy disc and a large computed cross-section below it using I(r) equals the squared Bessel Airy expression. Label the curve 'computed intensity'; keep the point, lens, disc, and curve aligned horizontally. The curve gently pulses with the source.
scenes.narration: Start with one point source. In ideal widefield fluorescence, every point becomes a blur. The screen shows a bright centre with faint rings, an Airy pattern. This computed green curve is its intensity across the screen.

scenes.tts: Why does the point spread? Light diffracts at the objective opening. A finer pattern bends light through wider angles. The lens collects only a cone, so some information from fine detail misses the objective. Numerical aperture describes the width of the collected cone.
scenes.visual: Carry the same point, objective, detector, Airy disc, and computed curve. Animate several green rays spreading from the point. The blue objective accepts rays inside a blue cone while wider rays pass outside and fade. Grow a blue double-headed arc across the accepted cone and label it 'numerical aperture'. Keep faint particles moving along accepted rays.
scenes.narration: Why does the point spread? Light diffracts at the objective opening. A finer pattern bends light through wider angles. The lens collects only a cone, so some information from fine detail misses the objective. Numerical aperture describes the width of the collected cone.

scenes.tts: In this ideal lateral model, the Rayleigh distance equals zero point six one times emission wavelength, divided by numerical aperture. Emission wavelength is the colour released by the fluorescent label. In the ideal lateral model, the Rayleigh distance gets smaller with shorter emission wavelength or higher numerical aperture. It is one resolution convention, not a universal border.
scenes.caption: In this ideal lateral model, the Rayleigh distance equals 0.61 times emission wavelength, divided by numerical aperture. Emission wavelength is the colour released by the fluorescent label. In the ideal lateral model, the Rayleigh distance gets smaller with shorter emission wavelength or higher numerical aperture. It is one resolution convention, not a universal border.
scenes.visual: Keep the bench. Place a yellow formula card above the detector: 'd = 0.61 λem / NA' and label it 'Rayleigh, lateral'. Drive the picture from two animated controls: shortening a green wavelength slider narrows the computed Airy curve, then widening the blue collection cone narrows it again. A small yellow d bracket follows the curve's first minimum. Mark the plot 'computed'.
scenes.narration: In this ideal lateral model, the Rayleigh distance equals 0.61 times emission wavelength, divided by numerical aperture. Emission wavelength is the colour released by the fluorescent label. In the ideal lateral model, the Rayleigh distance gets smaller with shorter emission wavelength or higher numerical aperture. It is one resolution convention, not a universal border.

scenes.tts: Now restore both vesicles. Their separation is one hundred fifty nanometres. For the settings shown here, the displayed Rayleigh distance is about two hundred twenty-seven nanometres. Will the detector show two peaks, or one?
scenes.caption: Now restore both vesicles. Their separation is 150 nanometres. For the settings shown here, the displayed Rayleigh distance is about 227 nanometres. Will the detector show two peaks, or one?
scenes.visual: Restore both green vesicles at the same fixed positions. Show a yellow '150 nm' bracket between them and a second yellow 'd ≈ 227 nm' bracket beneath it. On the detector, show two faint dotted placeholders but no answer curve. Centre the question 'TWO PEAKS OR ONE?' above the detector. Green particles continue drifting from sources to the objective.
scenes.narration: Now restore both vesicles. Their separation is 150 nanometres. For the settings shown here, the displayed Rayleigh distance is about 227 nanometres. Will the detector show two peaks, or one?

scenes.visual: Hold the complete prediction frame for 4.5 seconds. Keep source positions, both yellow brackets, and 'TWO PEAKS OR ONE?' unchanged. Only the soft green emission shimmer and particles move; do not reveal any detector profile.

scenes.tts: Each source still makes its own blur. On the detector, their intensities add point by point. The two computed curves merge into one summed peak. At one hundred fifty nanometres, no dip survives between them. They are unresolved here, although other methods may separate them.
scenes.visual: Send light from both points through the same objective. Draw two thin green computed Airy cross-sections, one from each source, then add them point by point into one thick white summed curve. Transform the two dotted detector placeholders into one broad spot. Add the red label 'one recorded peak' only after the sum forms. Mark all three curves 'computed'.
scenes.narration: Each source still makes its own blur. On the detector, their intensities add point by point. The two computed curves merge into one summed peak. At one hundred fifty nanometres, no dip survives between them. They are unresolved here, although other methods may separate them.

scenes.tts: Move the sources apart. A shallow dip opens before they reach the Rayleigh distance. At that distance, the central dip is about one quarter of peak height. That clear dip is the convention for calling two points resolved. For two ideal points, the Rayleigh distance marks a clear dip, not the first appearance of two peaks.
scenes.visual: Carry the same bench and summed detector plot. Slide the vesicles apart continuously. Show the dip first appearing at about 175 nm, before the yellow d bracket, then deepening as the sources reach d ≈ 227 nm. At the bracket, label the computed sum 'Rayleigh: ≈26% dip'. Keep every curve computed and keep the source-to-curve alignment visible.
scenes.narration: Move the sources apart. A shallow dip opens before they reach the Rayleigh distance. At that distance, the central dip is about one quarter of peak height. That clear dip is the convention for calling two points resolved. For two ideal points, the Rayleigh distance marks a clear dip, not the first appearance of two peaks.

scenes.tts: Return the vesicles to one hundred fifty nanometres. The detector again records one peak. Software zoom enlarges that record. It cannot add detail the optics and camera never captured. Optical magnification before the camera can change sampling; that is a different operation. Bigger display pixels cannot recover a missing dip.
scenes.caption: Return the vesicles to 150 nanometres. The detector again records one peak. Software zoom enlarges that record. It cannot add detail the optics and camera never captured. Optical magnification before the camera can change sampling; that is a different operation. Bigger display pixels cannot recover a missing dip.
scenes.visual: Slide the vesicles back to 150 nm and smoothly merge the computed sum to one peak. Freeze the detector record, then send a copy to a display with its own pixel grid. Animate a yellow 'SOFTWARE ZOOM' control: the display pixels and one-peak curve expand together. Keep the detector record unchanged and place a red crossed-out dip between the enlarged curve's shoulders.
scenes.narration: Return the vesicles to 150 nanometres. The detector again records one peak. Software zoom enlarges that record. It cannot add detail the optics and camera never captured. Optical magnification before the camera can change sampling; that is a different operation. Bigger display pixels cannot recover a missing dip.

scenes.tts: To separate or interpret closer objects, change how information enters the record. A confocal pinhole asks which out-of-focus light reaches the detector. Super-resolution asks how illumination or glowing molecules can encode closer detail. Electron microscopy replaces light with a different probe. Each change answers a measurement problem and brings new limits.
scenes.visual: Zoom back to the full carried bench. Transform only the centre measurement element in three quick, labelled states while the two vesicles stay fixed: a blue pinhole rejects drifting out-of-focus green haze; a yellow striped-light block sweeps across the sources, then sparse sources blink one at a time; finally a grey electron-beam block replaces the light objective. Label these states 'confocal', 'super-resolution', and 'electron microscopy'. Keep each icon schematic and never draw molecular structures.
scenes.narration: To separate or interpret closer objects, change how information enters the record. A confocal pinhole asks which out-of-focus light reaches the detector. Super-resolution asks how illumination or glowing molecules can encode closer detail. Electron microscopy replaces light with a different probe. Each change answers a measurement problem and brings new limits.

scenes.tts: A microscope image is a measurement, not the specimen itself. Before trusting one, ask what was labelled, what the instrument could separate, and what the detector recorded. Software zoom makes the same record bigger. Software zoom cannot add detail the optics and camera never captured.
scenes.visual: Restore the original two-vesicle optical bench in a clean, dimmed state. Draw three small white checks along the signal path: 'label', 'separation', 'record'. Then fade the bench while the final end-card line remains large and centred: 'Software zoom cannot add detail the measurement never captured.' Keep a slow green shimmer behind the text until the scene ends.
scenes.narration: A microscope image is a measurement, not the specimen itself. Before trusting one, ask what was labelled, what the instrument could separate, and what the detector recorded. Software zoom makes the same record bigger. Software zoom cannot add detail the optics and camera never captured.
